Auto-Parts Supplier Bosch Backs Guidance as Cost Cutting Continues
By Dominic Chopping
Germany's Robert Bosch still expects sales and profitability to increase this year as it works through a strategic plan to cut costs while investing in new technology.

The company, one of the world's largest auto-parts suppliers, said Wednesday that it expects global economic uncertainties to continue delaying investment decisions while ramping up competitive pressure. But its targets of 2%-5% sales growth and 4%-6% earnings before interest and taxes margin remain intact.
By the end of the year, it anticipates positive free cash flow of at least 1% of sales revenue.

Earlier this year, the company said it would cut 13,000 jobs by the end of 2030, citing tough market conditions, heightened competition and difficulties penetrating markets with new technologies, with the cuts coming on top of 9,000 redundancies announced the year before.
It has also previously said that it will lean into artificial intelligence to boost productivity gains in manufacturing and improve supply-chain efficiency to cut costs.

"Bosch is rigorously pursuing its growth strategy despite global uncertainties and is capitalizing on opportunities in new technologies, business areas, and emerging markets," Chief Financial Officer Markus Forschner said Wednesday.

"That is why our focus for the second half of the year will continue to be on increasing competitiveness and ensuring the company maintains its robust presence. Our goal is to further reduce costs and complexity."
The company said war in the Middle East and the continuing conflict in Ukraine contributed to slowing global growth in the first half, while exchange-rate effects also dampened its sales development.

Earnings in its main mobility business were weighed by stagnant automotive production in the first six months of the year, as well as 270 million euros ($309.2 million) of one-off costs that were mainly related to impairment losses on production facilities as the global ramp-up of electromobility lags expectations.

First-half sales revenue rose 3.6% on year to 46.4 billion euros, as growth in its industrial technology and energy and building technology businesses offset sales declines in mobility and consumer goods.
Bosch reported EBIT in the period of 2.2 billion euros, down from 2.3 billion euros a year ago and resulting in a margin of 4.6%, down from 5.1%.
The earnings report represents the first time Bosch has published interim earnings.
The company had around 406,225 employees as of June 30, down from 412,774 at Dec. 31.
